learning_objective: 🎯 Discover the chemistry of keeping clothes clean! Learn how soaps work, the secrets to removing tough stains, and how to make fabrics last longer.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Both clean fabrics by breaking the surface tension of water to lift dirt. However, detergents are better because they work well even in 'hard water' (water with high minerals), whereas natural soaps leave a scum.

Treat stains immediately! Don't rub hard, dab gently. Identify the stain first (protein stains like blood need cold water; grease needs hot water and soap). Always test the chemical on a hidden corner of the fabric first.
Washing involves soaking (to loosen dirt), applying detergent, applying friction or agitation (rubbing, beating, or machine spinning), rinsing thoroughly with clean water, and extracting water.
Starching gives cotton crispness. Ironing removes wrinkles and restores the shape of the garment. The temperature of the iron must match the fabric (high for cotton, very low for silk/synthetics).
Clothes must be completely dry before storing to prevent mildew (fungus). Woolens and silks should be packed with naphthalene balls or dried neem leaves to protect them from moths and insects.

fun_activity.title: ☕ The Stain First-Aid
fun_activity.instructions: Next time you drop a drop of tea or ketchup on your shirt, run it under cold water immediately from the *back* of the stain (to push it out, not deeper in). See how much easier it washes off compared to a dried stain!

exam_tips: 📌 Always state that detergents are superior to soaps because they don't form scum in hard water.
📌 Remember the golden rule for blood/egg (protein) stains: NEVER use hot water, it will cook the protein into the fabric. Use cold water.
📌 Mildew (fungus) attacks cotton/linen if left damp, while moths attack wool and silk.
quick_recap: ⭐ Proper care significantly extends the lifespan of expensive apparel.
⭐ Dry cleaning uses chemical solvents instead of water to clean delicate fabrics like silk and heavy wool.
⭐ Always read the 'Care Label' on clothes before washing or ironing them.
